3D Visual Effects (VFX) | Live-Action Footage Manipulation | 3D Camera Tracking & Compositing
#Blender
#AfterEffects

A VFX project addressing five challenges within a single moving tabletop shot: adding a reflective metal sphere, removing unwanted details, replacing a framed picture with glass reflections, integrating metal rings around an existing object, and introducing an original addition. The project combines Blender, Mocha AE and After Effects for 3D rendering, footage cleanup and image replacement.

Course(s)

2.3 3D VFX (Light)

Category

Visual Effects, Camera Tracking, Planar Tracking, 3D Modeling, Texturing, Compositing

Related link(s)

Raw footage: Original assignment video for comparison​

Duration

4 weeks

Challenge

The assignment required five different interventions to remain consistent within the same camera move. A metal ball needed to sit on the central black cage; the hole on the left side of the table and the tracking markers required removal; the framed picture needed a replacement that preserved reflective glass and foreground overlaps; two metal rings needed to fit around the stacked cylinders on the right; and an additional creative element needed to extend the scene. Together, these tasks required control over perspective, reflections, shadows and occlusion.

Process

For the metal ball, the Blender scene uses a tracked camera and aligned reference geometry to position the sphere above the cage. Scratched-aluminium textures control its colour, roughness and surface detail, while an HDRI provides environmental reflections. Shadow-catcher geometry supports its integration with the filmed surfaces. The tabletop cleanup uses fill sequences and paint elements in After Effects to replace unwanted areas with surrounding surface detail. These patches address the hole and tracking markers while following the moving shot. For the picture replacement, Mocha AE supplies a planar track of the frame, and Corner Pin effects fit the “Turkey Mentioned” image to its changing perspective. A separate reflection layer preserves the appearance of glass over the inserted image, while foreground masking maintains the overlaps of objects in front of the frame. The rings use torus geometry in Blender and sit around the stacked cylinders. Reflective shading connects them visually to the sphere, while shadow-catcher geometry represents the existing cylindrical surfaces. The open-ended fifth challenge takes the form of a cigarette-themed prop arrangement. A textured cigarette pack, an ashtray and cigarettes occupy the tabletop, introducing additional shapes and material finishes.

Solution

The final shot places the metal sphere on the black cage at the centre of the table, replaces the framed picture with a Turkey meme, and adds a cigarette pack, ashtray and cigarette to the foreground arrangement. Across the camera move, the additions occupy distinct positions within the scene: the sphere acts as the central reflective element, the picture provides a personalised detail, and the smaller props extend the tabletop composition. The completed sequence is presented as a 3840 × 2160 video at 25 frames per second.

WanderWood - Indie Music Festival | Brand Identity | Graphic Design
#Photoshop

Wanderwood is an outdoor music festival concept bringing folk, soft indie and alternative music into a woodland setting. Its graphics combine forest photography, newspaper clippings and mismatched cutout letters, taking inspiration from scrapbooks and memories of camping trips. The poster, social posts and merchandise share an earthy, handmade look that reflects the festival’s relaxed atmosphere.

Course(s)

1.1 Graphic Design Basics

Category

Brand Identity, Digital Collage, Poster Design, Social Media Graphics, Merchandise Design

Related link(s)

-

Duration

6 weeks

Challenge

The challenge is to capture the feeling of spending a few days outdoors with music, friends and room to wander. The graphics need to feel playful and loosely assembled while keeping the lineup, dates and location easy to find. Each format also requires a different arrangement: a poster holds the full event announcement, social banners introduce the festival, and the Instagram carousel gives more space to the artists.

Process

The visual research brings together camping photographs, forest landscapes, vintage posters, botanical collages and old paper textures. Deep greens and warm orange sit alongside cream, mustard and dark blue, drawing colour from the woods and the materials of a scrapbook.

The festival name uses individual cutout letters with different typefaces, sizes and colours. Their uneven placement gives the lettering a handmade quality, with scraps of paper and tape behind it. A bear carrying a backpack and rolled sleeping mat provides a smaller logo that connects directly to the camping theme. In Photoshop, overlapping photographs form an imagined landscape of forests, mountains and waterfalls. Torn edges expose newspaper and coloured paper beneath the images, while grain and colour adjustments help the separate pieces feel like part of the same collage. The poster uses the same cutout lettering for Aurora, Pomme and Phoebe Bridgers, with the dates and location placed on cream strips of paper.

The Instagram carousel continues the landscape across three panels, placing artist photographs among the paper layers. Facebook and Twitter headers give more space to the festival name. Clothing and tote-bag mockups show the collage lettering on fabric, while the cup uses the simpler bear logo.

Solution

Wanderwood’s graphics give the festival a setting and a mood before the viewer reads the details. The woodland photographs suggest somewhere to explore, and the paper scraps make the artwork feel collected and personal. Artist portraits connect that setting to the music, while clear information strips keep the practical details readable. Across the different pieces, the recurring lettering, textures and colours make the festival easy to recognise without repeating the same layout.

Piece by Piece | Character & Product Animation | In Progress
#Blender

An ongoing 3D product advertisement bringing together my Zooble-inspired eyeshadow palette and a modeled, rigged version of the character from The Amazing Digital Circus. The project expands the Piece by Piece packaging concept into a character-led sequence, combining product presentation with expressive physical acting.

Course(s)

[ Personal Project ]

Category

3D Animation, Character Modeling, Character Rigging, Product Animation, Visual Storytelling

Related link(s)

3D Animation: Eyeshadow Product Advertisement (Ongoing)​

Duration

Ongoing

Challenge

The challenge is to develop a product advertisement in which character performance and product presentation support one another. The palette already has a detailed visual identity, so the animation needs to give it a narrative context while leaving enough space for its design to be appreciated. Zooble’s asymmetrical construction introduces another challenge: the character combines rigid geometric pieces, narrow limbs, curved components, and different hand shapes, each requiring an appropriate approach to movement. Translating a human performance into this unusual body means adapting poses and gestures while preserving their intention and readability. The project also involves coordinating several stages of production, from reference recording and movement planning to modeling, rigging, and animation, with repeated adjustments as the character is tested in more demanding poses.

Process

Development began with preparing the character and product for animation in Blender. I modeled Zooble’s contrasting body parts, recreating the triangular head, mismatched eyes, colorful torso, and varied limbs to establish a recognizable silhouette. The character was then rigged with controls for posing the body, face, and individual appendages. Particular attention has gone into how the different components respond to movement, balancing flexible sections with pieces that need to retain their shape. Pose testing has helped identify areas requiring further refinement, including bends, joint connections, and the behavior of the character’s more unusual limbs. To plan the performance, I recorded live-action reference of myself kneeling beside a container, searching inside it, and making broad arm gestures. Selected frames were arranged into a visual sequence, with simplified drawings over the photographs to study body position, changes in balance, and the direction of each action. These drawings reduce the movement to its main shapes, making it easier to translate the performance into Zooble’s proportions. In Blender, a simple box provides a reference for the character’s interaction and helps establish contact, reach, and staging. The current work focuses on developing clear poses and refining the rig alongside the animation. The existing palette model, including its controllable opening lid, provides the product asset for the developing advertisement.

Solution

The project is currently in production, with a modeled and rigged character, a prepared product asset, recorded acting reference, and initial interaction poses established. At this stage, the work demonstrates the progression from a static packaging concept toward an animated presentation, alongside the testing needed to make an unconventional character perform convincingly. Further development will focus on refining movement, timing, character–object contact, and the product reveal before completing lighting and rendering. The intended result is a short fan-made advertisement that brings the palette’s graphic identity and Zooble’s character performance together within the wider cosmetics project.

Wingardium Laviosa in Lego | Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone | Fan Animation
#Blender
#Unity
#AdobeIllustrator

A short, LEGO-style Harry Potter cinematic created using Blender, Adobe Illustrator, and Unity. I worked with existing LEGO models from Mecabricks to build a classroom in Hogwarts, designed custom character textures, and brought everything together through animation, lighting, and camera work on Unity.

Course

2.4 Real-time 3D (ATO)

Category

Game Development, Real-Time Cinematics, 3D Modelling, Character Texturing, Animation

Link

Progress documentation:  YouTube playlist with final delivery.

Duration

4 weeks

Challenge

The challenge was to create a short cinematic in Unity using LEGO characters and environments. The project was divided into weekly stages, starting with building a scene in Blender and importing it into Unity, followed by character customization, UV mapping, texturing, lighting, camera work, and animation. The requirements included customizing at least two LEGO characters, creating multiple camera shots using Timeline and Cinemachine, and animating both characters and environmental objects. The final cinematic needed to combine these elements into a complete sequence with attention to scene composition, materials, lighting, and visual presentation. Drawing inspiration from the Harry Potter universe, I aimed to create a short, atmospheric sequence that captured the playful charm of LEGO while establishing a distinct sense of place and visual storytelling.

Process

I began by importing LEGO models and multiple base assets from Mecabricks into Blender, where I assembled the Hogwarts-inspired interior by arranging architectural elements and props to create a recognizable classroom setting. After importing the scene into Unity, I established the cinematic sequence using Timeline and Cinemachine, experimenting with camera angles, framing, and transitions to guide the viewer through the environment. I customized the LEGO characters through UV unwrapping and texture editing, developing individual facial expressions and clothing details. As the scene evolved, I refined the camera movements, adjusted materials and lighting, and incorporated character and environmental animations. Particular attention went into creating a warm, firelit atmosphere that complemented the setting and gave the cinematic a more immersive appearance.

Solution

The final result is a 12-second LEGO recreation of the Wingardium Leviosa scene from Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. The cinematic features Ron and Hermione practicing the spell, with two additional LEGO students modeled after me and my boyfriend, sitting behind them and reacting to Hermione successfully levitating the feather. Each character was customized through UV mapping and textures designed in Adobe Illustrator, giving them distinct faces and Hogwarts uniforms. All four characters were individually animated to recreate the spellcasting, reactions, and interactions within the scene. The floating feather and flickering fireplace were also animated to bring movement to the surrounding environment. To achieve the warm, dimly lit Hogwarts atmosphere, the scene used a combination of baked lighting, Light Probe Groups for dynamic objects, Reflection Probes for more accurate reflections, and a Global Volume for post-processing adjustments. Materials and lighting were refined to keep the LEGO surfaces visually consistent with the environment. Finally, Unity's Timeline and Cinemachine were used to coordinate character animations, camera movements, and shot transitions, bringing the different elements together into a complete cinematic sequence.

College Student Room │3D Model │ Environmental & Prop Design
#Blender

A 3D bedroom scene modeled in Blender, inspired by a combination of my university dorm and my old room back home. The project began as a collection of studies of everyday objects and gradually developed into a complete interior. Furniture, electronics, clothing, and personal belongings come together in a slightly cramped, lived-in space, using small details and intentional disorder to suggest the personality and routines of its occupant.

Course(s)

[ Personal Project ]

Category

3D Modeling, Prop Design, 3D Environment Design, Material Creation, Lighting, Environmental Storytelling

Link

Project showcase:  Teen Room on ArtStation.​

Duration

~ 5 months, on and off

Challenge

The challenge was to bring a varied collection of individually modeled props together in a convincing bedroom environment. The project began with observing and recreating real objects around me, providing opportunities to practice different shapes, construction methods, and surface details. As the collection grew, the focus expanded from individual models to how they could work together within one space. Furniture and electronics needed structured forms, while clothing, curtains, and other fabric elements required softer, less regular surfaces. Another challenge was balancing detail with readability: the room needed to feel crowded and personal while still allowing individual objects to be appreciated. Inspired by my university dorm and my room back home, the aim was to capture the experience of fitting everyday life into a single room, where studying, relaxing, getting dressed, and pursuing hobbies all share the same limited space.

Process

Development began with modeling everyday objects, gradually expanding into furniture, desk accessories, clothing, and decorative elements. Different modeling approaches were used across the collection. Mirror modifiers supported symmetrical forms, while Array modifiers handled repeated elements. Subdivision Surface modifiers refined curved objects, including the mug and ashtray, and combinations of Bevel, Solidify, and subdivision helped develop rounded edges and surface thickness across other meshes. Fabric studies included cloth simulation setups for curtain and draped surfaces, while the rug combined a particle system with subdivision to introduce surface texture. A Geometry Nodes setup was also used for the fairy lights. Materials combined BlenderKit assets that I adapted and UV mapped with textures created from image sources, allowing wood, fabric, plastic, metal, and smaller printed details to contribute to the room’s variety. A procedural moonlit skydome was created with shader nodes for the view through the window. As the environment developed, object placement became part of the storytelling, with cables, loosely folded clothes, and everyday clutter suggesting ongoing use. Lighting and camera composition brought these separate studies together for the final Cycles renders.

Solution

The finished project is a detailed bedroom environment that presents a broad collection of original prop models within a shared setting. Larger furniture establishes the room’s layout, while smaller objects give each area its own purpose and character. The desk brings together electronics and everyday accessories; clothing and fabric elements soften the surrounding structure; and personal belongings, including the guitar, plants, and printed details, suggest the occupant’s interests. Small placement decisions help the room feel temporarily unoccupied rather than carefully staged: a cigarette remains in the ashtray, cables emerge beneath the desk, and the chair is turned toward the door as though someone has just stood up. The final presentation includes different lighting treatments, closer views, and a solid-shaded overview, showing both the atmosphere of the environment and the modeling behind it. Together, these views turn a series of individual object studies into a cohesive showcase of prop modeling, material work, and environmental storytelling.

Paranoia [ DEMO ] │Game Design│Prototype Development
#Unity

Paranoia is a first-person psychological horror game set in a late-1990s supermarket. Inspired by a true story, the game follows Ashley, a young cashier, whose ordinary evening takes a disturbing turn. With a focus on anxiety, social pressure, and unreliable perception, the game explores the uncertainty of whether danger is real or a product of fear.

Course(s)

2.1 Principles of Game Design (KdG) & Game Design with Gavin Yeo (ELVTR)

Category

Game Design, Game Development, Narrative Design, Level Design, Game Design Document (GDD)

Link(s)

Playable demo:  Paranoia on itch.io

​

Game Design Document:  37-page design document

 

Recognition:  ELVTR certificate and instructor recommendation.

Duration

14 weeks total (6 weeks at KdG + 8 weeks at ELVTR)

Challenge

The original assignment for Principles of Game Design was to develop an original game concept, document its design in a Game Design Document (GDD), and build a playable prototype demonstrating its main mechanics, visual style, and gameplay. Development followed several milestones covering concept creation, story, game world, player interactions, and level design. The project was later revisited during an additional Game Design course at ELVTR, with the aim of developing the initial concept into a more complete and structured GDD. This involved applying professional game design principles to the game's vision, Mechanics, Dynamics & Aesthetics (MDA), gameplay loops, systems, level design, narrative, and balancing.

The chosen concept was Paranoia, a psychological horror game where the challenge was to create tension without relying on combat, monsters, or conventional jump scares, instead using player interactions and social situations to make ordinary encounters feel increasingly uncomfortable.

Process

Development began with the game's concept, story, characters, and PSX-inspired visual direction. A supermarket environment was assembled in Unity using sourced 3D assets, with custom interactions, dialogue, and gameplay systems developed in C#. The initial prototype focused on the core experience: basic cashier tasks, environmental inspection, dialogue choices, and a breathing mini-game triggered by stressful encounters. These systems were developed alongside the game's narrative to make Ashley's anxiety part of the gameplay rather than something explained through dialogue alone. During the ELVTR course, the original GDD was expanded and reworked using the MDA framework, gameplay loops, a Composure system, branching narrative paths, and more detailed level designs. Feedback from instructor Gavin Yeo helped refine the relationship between the game's story and mechanics, with particular attention to player agency, emotional pacing, and how the design could eventually be implemented.

Solution

The project resulted in a playable Unity prototype and a 37-page Game Design Document covering the larger game concept. The demo introduces the player to Ashley's routine through a short cashier training sequence before allowing exploration of the supermarket. Inspectable objects reveal her inner thoughts and personal background, while a dialogue system introduces choices during conversations with NPCs. A breathing mini-game turns moments of panic into an interactive challenge, requiring the player to maintain control as the encounter becomes more stressful. The game uses low-poly PSX-style visuals, dark lighting, and retro-inspired UI to establish its unsettling atmosphere. The prototype focuses on testing these core systems and how they work together to communicate the game's psychological themes. The expanded GDD develops the concept further, introducing a Composure system that affects perception, dialogue, and player control, alongside branching storylines, multiple endings, and a three-act narrative structure. Level layouts, character profiles, environmental storytelling, game loops, and audio direction were also documented to guide future development. The project received an ELVTR Certificate of Completion for Exceptional Performance, along with a recommendation letter from instructor Gavin Yeo, highlighting the game's worldbuilding, narrative integration, and application of game design principles.

Piece by Piece (Eyeshadow Palette) | 3D Product Design | The Amazing Digital Circus Fan Art
#Blender
#Photoshop
#AdobeIllustrator

A fan-made eyeshadow palette inspired by Zooble from The Amazing Digital Circus, combining vector illustration, packaging design, and 3D modeling. Every graphic element was created manually in Adobe Illustrator, assembled into packaging artwork in Photoshop, and applied to a palette modeled in Blender. Titled Piece by Piece, the concept translates Zooble’s mismatched shapes, contrasting colors, and distinctive personality into a cohesive cosmetic product.

Course(s)

[ Personal project ]

Category

Mixed Media, Graphic Design, Vector Illustration, Packaging Design, Product Visualization, 3D Modeling

Related link(s)

3D Animation: Eyeshadow Product Advertisement (Ongoing)​

Duration

1 week in total (3 days for eyeshadow palette + 4 days for Zooble's 3D model)

Challenge

The challenge was to translate an existing character into an eyeshadow palette with its own visual identity. Zooble’s contrasting colors, irregular shapes, and assembled appearance offered a starting point, but these references needed to work across several different formats: the outer cover, interior artwork, shade arrangement, and three-dimensional packaging. The design needed to feel expressive and deliberately mismatched while maintaining a readable hierarchy for the product name, shade names, and supporting information. Another challenge was carrying the same visual language between Illustrator, Photoshop, and Blender. Individual illustrations had to function as parts of a larger composition, while the completed packaging needed to remain convincing when wrapped around a model and viewed from different angles. The aim was to create a complete fan-designed product whose connection to Zooble extended beyond simply placing the character on its cover.

Process

Development centered on building a collection of original graphic elements in Adobe Illustrator. These included character-inspired shapes, decorative motifs, patterns, and supporting symbols, allowing the packaging to draw from Zooble’s appearance throughout its design. The title Piece by Piece connected the product to the character’s assembled form and informed the fragmented, collage-like composition. Contrasting animal prints, stripes, grids, colorful shapes, and torn-paper effects were brought together in Photoshop to create the packaging artwork. A dark base provided contrast for the brighter elements and helped the typography remain readable within the layered design. The interior continued this visual language around the character image and the arrangement of 18 named shades, combining direct color references with playful names and varied surface appearances. The completed artwork was then transferred to Blender, where I modeled the palette’s case, lid, and recessed eyeshadow pans. Materials helped distinguish the printed packaging from the powder surfaces, with variations suggesting matte, shimmer, and glitter finishes. I also modeled Zooble, recreating the character’s asymmetrical silhouette and contrasting components as part of the project’s wider visual presentation. The palette lid was connected to an Empty controller so it could be opened and closed around its hinge, making it possible to present the exterior and interior through the same model. Open and closed product renders brought the illustration, packaging composition, and modeled form together.

Solution

The finished concept is an 18-shade eyeshadow palette with a visual identity built around contrast, fragmentation, and playful disorder. The outer cover introduces Piece by Piece through bold pink lettering and a layered collection of patterns and character-inspired elements. Opening the palette reveals an interior that carries those same motifs around the character artwork and shade layout, creating continuity between the outside and inside of the product. The colors, names, and varied powder finishes extend the theme into the makeup itself, making the shade collection part of the design. The 3D presentation demonstrates how the flat artwork works as a complete object, showing the packaging’s thickness, the recessed pans, and the relationship between the lid and base. The controllable lid supports both open and closed views and provides a foundation for further presentation work. The result brings individually created vector assets, Photoshop composition, and Blender modeling together in one finished product concept, showcasing a workflow that moves from illustration to packaging and three-dimensional visualization.

AURA Lamp Advertisement Scene | 3D Modeling | Environmental Design
#Blender
#Photoshop

A product design and 3D visualization project that started with a simple paper cube and developed into Aura Light, a conceptual mood lamp. The project combines physical prototyping, branding, environmental modelling, and rendering, with the final advertisement presented in a realistic 3D bus stop scene.

Course

2.1 Prototyping

Category

Product Visualization, 3D Environment Design, Branding, Prototyping

Link(s)

Prototyping portfolio:  Pages 6-11​

Duration

~1 week

Challenge

The assignment introduced the fundamentals of prototyping by combining physical construction with digital 3D modelling. The initial task was to build a precise 4 × 4 × 4 cm cube from a single sheet of A4 paper, then explore how the same geometry could be recreated digitally and converted back into a printable paper model. The project was expanded into a product design and advertising exercise, requiring an original concept, promotional material, and a realistic 3D setting in which to present it. This led to Aura Light, a minimalist, paper-inspired mood lamp designed to switch between cold, neutral, and warm lighting. The main challenge was to develop a consistent visual identity while connecting physical prototyping, product design, and environmental visualization into one project.

Process

The physical prototype began with a hand-drawn net of six connected squares and additional folding tabs. The paper was cut and temporarily assembled with tape to check the proportions before the edges were permanently glued. For the product's branding, an A3 poster was designed in Canva using a sage green and beige colour palette, organic swirl patterns, repeating typography, and hand-drawn illustrations. Black outlines and layered paper textures were used to give the design a handcrafted appearance. The advertisement was then placed in a bus stop environment modelled in Blender. Particular attention went into making the scene feel like a believable public space, from separate material transitions between the pavement and road to raised tactile guidance strips that interact naturally with the lighting. Dirt, rust, and weathering were added around stone joints and metal supports, while overhanging vegetation helped balance the industrial structure with its surroundings. An Antwerp transit map, schedule signage, glass panels, and a trash bin were included to complete the setting. Materials, shadows, and camera composition were refined to give the final render a realistic appearance. To complete the prototyping cycle, Blender's Export Paper Model add-on was used to unfold the digital cube into a printable template. The pattern was then printed, cut, folded, and assembled, with careful attention to edge alignment and folding accuracy.

Solution

The finished work consists of a physical cube prototype, a conceptual mood lamp, an A3 promotional poster, a realistic Blender advertisement render, and a reconstructed paper model exported from the digital version. The final advertisement presents Aura Light as a product that could naturally appear in an everyday urban setting, with the campaign's visual identity carried through from the product illustration to the billboard. The detailed environment provides a convincing context for the design rather than displaying it as an isolated mockup. The reconstructed paper model completes the physical-to-digital-to-physical workflow, demonstrating how Blender geometry can be translated into a printable object while maintaining its intended proportions. Together, the deliverables turn a basic construction exercise into a product concept with its own branding, physical prototypes, and advertising presentation.

Anıtkabir: The Revival | Game Design & Development | 3D Modeling
#Unity
#Blender
#PremierePro

A first-person historical puzzle game developed in Unity, inspired by Anıtkabir, the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in Ankara, Turkey. The experience combines exploration, historical storytelling, and interactive puzzles, allowing visitors to discover the stories of fallen soldiers and uncover forgotten memories throughout the monument.

Course(s)

1.3 Fusion Challenge 2

Category

Game Design, Unity Development, 3D Environment Design, 3D Modeling, Interactive Storytelling, Puzzle Design

Link(s)

Playable game:  Anıtkabir: The Revival on itch.io

​

Gameplay overview:  6-page overview of the game

Duration

12 weeks

Challenge

The challenge was to design and develop an interactive 3D ghost museum for a fictional theme park. The museum needed to feature a unique collection of ghosts with their own stories, filmed and integrated into a virtual environment. Visitors had to be able to explore freely, interact with objects and characters, and experience atmospheric lighting and visual effects. With this brief in mind, the concept took a historical approach, exploring how a monument could become a more interactive and engaging experience without losing its cultural significance. This led to Anıtkabir: The Revival, a first-person puzzle game set in Anıtkabir, the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. Rather than using ghosts for horror, the game introduces the spirits of fallen soldiers whose stories unfold through exploration and memory-related tasks. The aim was to encourage visitors to engage with the history of Anıtkabir on a more personal level, combining historical storytelling with puzzles and environmental interactions while remaining respectful of the monument's significance.

Process

Development began with research into Anıtkabir's architecture, history, and symbolism, followed by concept planning and 3D modelling in Blender. The original assets were then imported into Unity to build the Lion Road, Hall of Honor, and Projection Room environments. Most of the development focused on programming the gameplay systems in C#. These included proximity-based interactions, an inventory and object-retrieval system, and a contextual dialogue manager with different responses based on the player's progress and carried items. Additional scripts handled task completion, puzzle validation, scene transitions, and the conditions for triggering different endings. Custom UI elements, interaction sounds, and cinematic sequences were implemented using Unity Timeline, camera animations, CanvasGroups, and TextMeshPro. Several technical issues were addressed along the way, particularly managing player controls during conversations and cutscenes. The environment was also refined through lighting, atmospheric effects, and Shader Graph experiments, including a custom wind animation for tree leaves that weren't responding to Unity's default wind settings. For the Projection Room, an original historical video was produced through costume preparation, filming, and editing in Adobe Premiere Pro before being integrated into Unity as an interactive projection.

Solution

The finished project is a first-person historical puzzle game set in a fully modelled recreation of Anıtkabir, with three main areas to explore and two possible endings. The experience begins on the Lion Road, lined with 24 lion statues, ten of which can be interacted with to discover historical facts. A mechanic inspired by the pathway's symbolism discourages visitors from looking too far upward while walking, temporarily stopping movement and displaying a red vignette to simulate stumbling. Inside the Hall of Honor, three ghost soldiers share their stories and ask visitors to recover personal belongings: a medal, a photograph, and a revolver. These tasks can be completed in any order, with the soldiers responding differently to correct items, incorrect items, or empty hands. A password-protected door leads to the final area, with an optional hint directing players toward the dates engraved on Atatürk's memorial. In the Projection Room, visitors activate a projector to watch an original live-action historical video. The experience concludes with either a Good Ending, featuring a fireworks sequence, or a Neutral Ending, depending on whether all three soldiers' tasks were completed. The result combines historical storytelling, exploration, and interactive puzzles into a museum experience where learning comes from actively engaging with the environment rather than simply observing it.

Mortal Balance (CrazyGames x Construct Game Jam Entry) | 2D Character Art | Game UI Design
#Procreate

Mortal Balance is a narrative-driven 2D game about the damage that comes with having too much power. The player takes the role of Insik, Protector of Life, in a conflict with Samara, Guider of the Dead. Both believe they protect humanity, but their attacks endanger the mortal world beneath them. Created in a team of two for the CrazyGames × Construct Game Jam.

Course(s)

CrazyGames x Construct Game Jam (June, 2026)

Category

2D Game Art, Character Design, Animation, Narrative Design, Scriptwriting

Related link(s)

Mortal Balance: Test out our entry on CrazyGames 

Duration

4 days

Challenge

The jam’s theme, “Overpowered,” raises a question: what happens when winning a fight means harming the people being protected? The story needs to give both characters a reason to believe they are right. Insik sees life as a gift that deserves protection, including its hardships. Samara sees prolonged suffering as cruelty and takes souls early out of mercy. Their disagreement needs to carry through the dialogue, character designs and player choices, so the consequences feel connected to their beliefs.

Process

Character profiles establish each figure’s motives, loyalties and contradictions before the script develops their confrontation. Insik’s devotion to divine order makes him protective but unwilling to question authority. Samara’s empathy drives her rebellion, yet she assumes the right to decide when another person’s life should end. The dialogue draws on these tensions, with each character challenging the other’s idea of mercy.

A paper storyboard maps the opening, arena view, alternating dialogue, choices, attacks and ending. The script develops this structure into five rounds with different responses and consequences. Two resources, Mortal Balance and Clash Pressure, connect the decisions to the outcome: excessive force damages the world, while too much restraint leaves Samara free to continue. The character portraits, gameplay sprites and animations are hand-drawn in Procreate. Insik’s white wings, gold accessories and warm colours draw on angelic imagery. Samara’s hood, cool skin and dark purple clothing give her a contrasting silhouette. Their dialogue frames continue these differences through gold ornament and wing details for Insik, and purple borders with branch-like decoration for Samara.

Adobe Illustrator was used to bring together the dialogue boxes, nameplates, choice buttons and resource display. Programming, sound design and integration in Construct 3 was handled by my teammate.

Solution

Mortal Balance makes restraint part of the fight. The player needs enough force to confront Samara while preserving the world Insik claims to defend. Branching dialogue and multiple endings show the cost of that balance, including a hollow victory where defeating an opponent undermines the purpose of fighting. The character art gives the conflict two distinct faces, while the writing leaves room to question both of them.
